sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
In a non-linear capacitor the charge is not simply proportional to voltage, so a single number \(Q/V\) is not enough. The useful quantity for small signals is the **slope** of the Q–V curve at the bias point: the **small-signal (incremental) capacitance** \(C = dQ/dV\). Superimpose a small wiggle \(v\) on a DC bias \(V_0\), and the extra charge is approximately \(C(V_0)\,v\).

Junction and MOS capacitors behave this way, and that is why their capacitance changes with bias, which is exactly how a varactor tunes a radio. Large-signal ratio \(Q/V\) and small-signal slope \(dQ/dV\) are generally different numbers.
sections.figure_alt: Curved Q-V characteristic with a tangent line at the bias point labeled slope = C.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ C(V_0) = \left.\frac{dQ}{dV}\right|_{V = V_0} \]
\[ Q(V_0 + v) \approx Q(V_0) + C(V_0)\,v \]
Small-signal current: \(i = C(V_0)\,\dfrac{dv}{dt}\).
If \(Q = kV^n\), then \(C = nkV^{n-1}\), and \(Q/V = kV^{n-1}\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A device has \(Q(V) = 2\times10^{-12}\sqrt{V}\) coulombs (with \(V\) in volts). At \(V_0 = 4\ \mathrm{V}\):
\[ C = \frac{dQ}{dV} = \frac{2\times10^{-12}}{2\sqrt{V_0}} = \frac{10^{-12}}{2} = 0.5\ \mathrm{pF} \]
The large-signal ratio \(Q/V = 2\times10^{-12}\cdot2/4 = 1\ \mathrm{pF}\) is twice as big. Using it for small-signal analysis would be wrong.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using \(Q/V\) instead of \(dQ/dV\).
- Evaluating the derivative at the wrong bias point.
- Assuming the small-signal model holds for big swings; it is only a tangent-line approximation.
- Forgetting the chain rule when \(Q\) depends on a power of \((V_0 - V)\).

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Junction capacitance, MOS C–V curves and diode diffusion capacitance are all non-linear capacitors. In each case the small-signal model uses the slope at the operating point, exactly as here.
